title: Week 31 Check-In · Cross-Text Comparison
description: This week you compared two of the year's novels on one theme, organized the comparison by categories, read three real primary sources, analyzed a whole poem, and reviewed the year's grammar, roots and spelling.
chapters: The five novels + three primary sources

questions.label: Comparison Sentence
questions.text: Which comparison sentence is written correctly?
options: Although Kit Tyler hides her friendship with Hannah. Jack Flagg tells the captain the truth.
Although Kit Tyler hides her friendship with Hannah, Jack Flagg tells the captain the truth.
Kit Tyler hides her friendship with Hannah, Jack Flagg tells the captain the truth.
Although Kit Tyler hides her friendship with Hannah; Jack Flagg tells the captain the truth.
questions.from: 31.1–31.2 Grammar (comparison sentences: although); 31.3 Daily Oral Language model
questions.status: replaced (the old item’s ‘right’ sentence was a lesson-made claim about Praiseworthy; now a punctuation choice)

questions.label: Combine with While
questions.text: Combine these two sentences into one comparison sentence that begins with While.
questions.excerpt: Kit Tyler stands trial in Wethersfield. Johnny Tremain carries messages in Boston.
questions.key: While Kit Tyler stands trial in Wethersfield, Johnny Tremain carries messages in Boston. (While opens the sentence; a comma ends the while clause.)
questions.from: 31.2 Daily Oral Language model; 31.2 Grammar Show What You Know
questions.status: fixed (same skill; the old pair used a lesson-made claim)

questions.label: Semicolon
questions.text: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
options: Isaac loses his home; and Jack leaves his by choice.
Isaac loses; his home and Jack leaves his by choice.
Isaac loses his home; Jack leaves his by choice.
Isaac loses his home, Jack; leaves his by choice.
questions.status: replaced (was ‘write a concluding sentence’; the essay items cover writing)

questions.label: Root Meaning
options: tract
fort
curr / curs
spect
questions.from: 31.1–31.2 Morphology (year-long root families); the week’s word game

questions.label: Word Parts
questions.text: manu means hand and script means write. What is a manuscript?
options: something written by hand
a map drawn by hand
a book about hands
a printed newspaper

questions.label: Context Clues
questions.text: Read the lines from Bayard Taylor’s Eldorado (1850). What does porter mean here?
questions.excerpt: I asked the landlord whether he could send a porter for our trunks. “There is none belonging to the house,” said he; “every man is his own porter here.”
options: a person who carries bags and trunks
a ship’s captain
the owner of a hotel
a newspaper reporter
questions.from: 31.2 Primary Source B (Taylor); 31.4 word game (port = carry)
questions.status: replaced (was ‘choose any root and write a sentence’; now vocabulary in context)

questions.label: Cumulative Words
options: seperate
definately
occurred
embarass
questions.status: changed (the year’s tricky words; four options)

questions.label: Edit for Spelling
questions.text: Find and correct every misspelling. Write the sentences correctly.
questions.excerpt: Kit Tyler showed remarkable fortitued and persistance. Nevertheles, her notoreity as an accused witch came from the town’s ignorence.
questions.key: Kit Tyler showed remarkable fortitude and persistence. Nevertheless, her notoriety as an accused witch came from the town’s ignorance. (fortitude, persistence, Nevertheless, notoriety, ignorance)
questions.status: fixed (‘a witch accussed’ reworded; same five words)

questions.label: Word Families
questions.text: Which pair belongs to the same word family?
options: describe / descriptive
fortitude / tenacious
nevertheless / consequently
curious / current

questions.label: Source Types
questions.text: Which of these is a primary source?
options: Henry Bigler’s diary entry, written at Sutter’s Mill on January 24, 1848
By the Great Horn Spoon!, a novel published in 1963
the background card written by Optima for this week
a textbook chapter about the Gold Rush
questions.from: 31.2 What Good Readers Do and the three primary sources
questions.status: replaced (tested the invented ‘three eras’ secondary source)

questions.label: Comparison Claim
questions.text: Which comparison claim names both a similarity and a difference?
options: Both Kit and Jack are brave.
Kit lives in Connecticut, and Jack lives in Boston.
Both Kit and Jack find courage far from home; however, Kit’s costs her the town’s trust, while Jack’s costs him his gold.
Jack is braver than Kit.

questions.label: Poetry
questions.text: In “Buffalo Dusk,” why is the middle line so much longer than the others?
options: It is the only line where the buffaloes are alive, so it runs on like the herd.
Sandburg ran out of room on the page.
It rhymes with the first line.
It tells the year the poem was written.

questions.label: Category Paragraph
questions.text: Write one category paragraph from your essay (4–6 sentences): name the category, put both novels in it with evidence from each, and say why the difference matters. Underline two transition words.
questions.key: A category named first; both novels inside it with a real moment or exact words from each; at least one sentence of reasoning about why the difference matters; two transitions underlined.
questions.from: 31.1–31.4 Read Like a Writer (categories); 31.2–31.3 Comparison Project
questions.status: changed (was the four-step ‘comparison paragraph’; now the week’s category paragraph)

questions.label: The Other Side
questions.text: Write one sentence a reader who disagrees with your comparison claim might say. Then write one sentence that answers them with evidence from a book.
questions.key: A fair counter-claim, then an answer that uses a specific moment or exact words from one of the two novels.
